checks.claim: The textbook equation is 6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy -> C6H12O6 + 6O2
Atom count balances: left 6 C, 12 H, 18 O (6x2 + 6x1); right C6H12O6 (6 C, 12 H, 6 O) + 6O2 (12 O) = 6 C, 12 H, 18 O
Key: two glucose (2 x 6 C) need twelve CO2 (one C each)
Wrong choices two, six, twenty-four molecules are wrong (two = one per glucose; six = one glucose; twenty-four = doubled)
Context: CO2 is the only reactant carrying carbon; atoms are neither made nor lost in a chemical reaction
Key: photosynthesis stores light energy as chemical energy in glucose
checks.note: Grokipedia: glucose 'serves as the primary energy-storing molecule'; 'converting solar energy into chemical energy'. A plant's long-term store is mostly starch and sucrose built from glucose; 'in glucose' is the NGSS-level simplification ('stored in sugar') and is still true.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'new atoms in the glucose' (light brings energy, no atoms; atoms are conserved)
Wrong: 'light energy trapped in the chlorophyll' (chlorophyll absorbs light in the thylakoids and passes the energy on; it is not a store)
Wrong: 'heat energy held in the leaves'
Context: every atom of glucose comes from CO2 and water; light carries energy but no atoms
Theodor Wilhelm Engelmann was German (physiologist, botanist); 'German biologist' is fair
Early 1880s: 1881 Spirogyra test (bacteria gathered at the chloroplasts); 1882 prism (Zeiss micro-spectroscope) test on a green alga with oxygen-seeking bacteria
checks.note: Wikipedia and Grokipedia name Cladophora for the 1882 prism test; many textbooks say Spirogyra. The stem names no species and says 'early 1880s', so it survives the disagreement.

checks.claim: Key: bacteria crowded in the red and blue light, at the chloroplasts
checks.note: Grokipedia: clustered 'primarily in the red and blue regions'; Wikipedia: 'red and violet'. Textbook accounts (e.g. LibreTexts botany) describe the bacteria around the parts of the filament (chloroplast) lit red and blue; Wikipedia credits the work with showing the chloroplast as the site.

checks.claim: Wrong: chloroplasts in green and yellow; nuclei in either light (the nucleus is not where oxygen is made)
Context: chlorophyll absorbs red and blue most strongly, little green, so leaves look green
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'absorb light most strongly in the blue and red portions'; 'a poor absorber of green and near-green portions of the spectrum'. Grokipedia Chlorophyll: peaks ~430 nm and ~662 nm.

checks.claim: Ruben and Kamen with two colleagues (Merle Randall, J. L. Hyde), University of California (Berkeley), 1941
checks.note: Ruben, Randall, Kamen and Hyde, 'Heavy oxygen (O18) as a tracer in the study of photosynthesis', JACS 63 (1941) 877-879. Wikipedia (Martin Kamen): at Berkeley Kamen 'confirmed in 1941 that all of the oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from water, not carbon dioxide'.

checks.claim: Heavy oxygen (oxygen-18) is rare and has two extra neutrons (8 protons, 10 neutrons vs 8 in O-16)
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'eight protons and ten neutrons'; non-radioactive; about 0.2% of natural oxygen.

checks.claim: Key: only the heavy-water test gave heavy-oxygen-rich O2 (water 0.85% -> O2 0.86%; heavy CO2 0.68% with normal water -> O2 0.20%, not enriched)
Wrong: only heavy CO2; both equally; neither
Context: O2 in the same share as the water; the older belief that the oxygen came from CO2
checks.note: Kimball: Senebier concluded (erroneously) that CO2 is decomposed and its oxygen released.

checks.claim: Context: the equation is a net count; to free 6 O2 a plant splits 12 H2O and makes 6 new H2O
checks.note: Standard form 6CO2 + 12H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O; water splitting yields one O2 per two H2O.

checks.claim: Van Niel at Stanford's Hopkins Marine Station around 1930 (arrived 1928-1929)
checks.note: Encyclopedia.com: transferred 'in 1929'; Grokipedia C. B. van Niel: late 1928. 'Around 1930' is fine.

checks.claim: Purple sulfur bacteria build food from CO2 with light, use H2S in place of water, give off no oxygen
Key: sulfur in place of oxygen (elemental sulfur globules)
checks.note: Kimball: 'no oxygen is liberated ... but rather elemental sulfur'; Grokipedia C. B. van Niel: 'producing sulfur instead of oxygen'. The globules are stored in or just outside the cell and can be oxidized on to sulfate; 'give off ... in its place' is the textbook framing.

checks.claim: Wrong: hydrogen; sulfur dioxide; methane
checks.note: Purple sulfur bacteria can make a little hydrogen gas through hydrogenases (Grokipedia), but not as the product that takes oxygen's place in H2S photosynthesis (they keep the hydrogen). No sulfur dioxide or methane.

checks.claim: Context: van Niel argued in 1931 that plant oxygen comes from water; 1941 heavy-oxygen tests bore him out
checks.note: Wikipedia: his 1931 work 'predicted that H2O is the hydrogen donor in green plant photosynthesis and is oxidized to O2'; Grokipedia: 'a hypothesis confirmed experimentally in 1941'; Encyclopedia.com: confirmed by heavy-oxygen experiments.

checks.claim: Setup: 5 lb (about 2.3 kg, 'about 2 kilograms') willow shoot, 200 lb (91 kg) of oven-dried soil, five years, rain or distilled water only, perforated lid against dust
checks.note: Grokipedia: '200 pounds of oven-dried soil', 'a 5-pound willow shoot', 'rain or distilled water', 'a tin-plated iron lid perforated with small holes'; Kimball gives the metric figures.

checks.claim: Willow gained about 74 kg (169 lb 3 oz less 5 lb = 164 lb, 74.5 kg)
Key: soil about 57 g lighter (about 2 oz)
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'a loss of only about 2 ounces'; Kimball: 2 oz (57 g).

checks.claim: Wrong: 570 g, 37 kg, 74 kg
Context: he concluded water alone and did not consider the air; much of the wood came from CO2 in the air
checks.note: Kimball: 'He did not consider the possibility that gases in the air might be involved.' Grokipedia: mass 'arose solely from water'.

checks.claim: Dry wood is about half carbon by weight (about 50% C, 6% H, 44% O)
De Saussure: Swiss chemist; careful quantitative measurements; published 1804 (Recherches chimiques sur la vegetation)
checks.note: No Grokipedia page found; Wikipedia and EBSCO Research Starters ('Swiss chemist and plant physiologist'; Lavoisier's quantitative methods, replicates and controls).

checks.claim: Key: he showed plants get their carbon from CO2 in the air
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, not through uptake from humus in the soil'; EBSCO: leaves 'assimilate large amounts of carbon directly from that source'.

checks.claim: Wrong: humus; soil minerals; water drawn up by the roots
checks.note: EBSCO: he 'disproved Senebier's contention that plants obtain carbon dioxide from water absorbed from the soil'; minerals come from the soil but are not the carbon source. (Soil water carries a trace of dissolved carbon dioxide, but the choice reads as the water itself, which holds no carbon.)

checks.claim: Context: water holds no carbon; soil gives only small amounts of minerals
Van Helmont concluded the tree was made of water alone; rain or distilled water for five years
Key: the wood's hydrogen came from water (only water carries hydrogen in the equation; water is the hydrogen donor)
checks.note: EBSCO on de Saussure: 'water contributes the large amount of hydrogen present in plant dry matter'; Wikipedia (van Niel): H2O 'is the hydrogen donor in green plant photosynthesis'. No oxygen choice is offered, so the open question of how much of the wood's oxygen exchanges with water does not arise.

checks.claim: Wrong: carbon (from CO2 in air); carbon and hydrogen; calcium (from the soil)
checks.note: Grokipedia Wood ash: calcium 'typically comprising 15-20% by weight' of ash; the minerals come from the soil through the roots.

checks.claim: Context: carbon from CO2 in the air, calcium from the soil; he never considered the air
Priestley put a sprig of mint into air in which a candle had burned out on 17 August 1771; on the 27th (ten days later) another candle 'burned perfectly well in it'
checks.note: Priestley's own text: 'on the 17th of August 1771, I put a sprig of mint into a quantity of air, in which a candle had burned out, and found that, on the 27th of the same month, another candle burned perfectly well in it'.

checks.claim: Key: it burned perfectly well; wrong: out at once, feebly then died, flared then died
Context: divided spent air in two, a plant in one; a candle burned only in that part
checks.note: 'a candle would burn in the former, but not in the latter'.

checks.claim: Context: a mouse could live in air a plant had mended; plants restore air spoiled by burning and breathing
checks.note: Grokipedia: restored air shown by 'the survival of a mouse placed inside'; Priestley to Franklin, 1 July 1772: air 'rendered in the highest degree noxious by breathing is restored by sprigs of mint growing in it'. Paraphrase, not a quotation.

checks.claim: Jan Ingenhousz, Dutch-born physician; over 500 experiments in summer 1779; a rented country house near London (Southall Green)
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'a Dutch-born physician, plant physiologist, and chemist'; 'over 500 experiments that summer'; 'rented a country house near London'. Wikipedia: Southall Green, 1779.

checks.claim: Leaves sunk in jars of water gave bubbles of the restorative gas
Key: only in the sunshine; not in a warm room without sun
checks.note: Ingenhousz (via Grokipedia): 'no dephlogisticated air is obtained in a warm room, if the sun does not shine upon the jar containing the leaves'. The context paraphrases this as 'Ingenhousz wrote that', which is documented.

checks.claim: Wrong: only the warm room; both alike; neither
checks.note: Wikipedia: plants purify air 'only in clear day light, or in the sun shine'.

checks.claim: Context: only green parts gave the gas; the process is named for light
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'only the green portions of plants—such as leaves—released the restorative gas'.

unit_notes: All ten questions check out against the web. Equation atom count verified by hand: 6CO2 + 6H2O gives 6 C, 12 H, 18 O, and C6H12O6 + 6O2 gives 6 C, 12 H, 18 O. Engelmann's alga for the prism test is Cladophora by Wikipedia and Grokipedia (Spirogyra in many textbooks); the stem names neither, so it is safe. Ruben et al. used bicarbonate as the 'carbon dioxide'; that is a fair simplification.
